podcast.body: The idea for this landmark song originated from Johnny Cash's anecdote about a serviceman referring to his shoes, and was solidified when Perkins overheard an audience member exclaim, "Don't step on my suede!" Perkins wrote the song one night, playing his electric guitar unplugged to avoid disturbing his wife. He recorded it on December 19, 1955, and famously misspelled "suede" as "SWAD-A-D-E" because he did not know the correct spelling. The song became a massive cross-over hit, reaching number two on both Pop and Country charts and number five on the R&B chart. Perkins's version is rhythmically sophisticated, featuring a stop-time introduction that transitions from 6/4 time into 4/4, creating a unique tension and release dynamic. "Perkins found himself one night getting out of bed, playing his electric guitar unplugged, so as not to disturb his wife, and writing a song he called Blue Suede shoes."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.body: This was a hit for Karl Perkins. He may have missed an opportunity to have a hit follow-up to this song at Sun Records when he reportedly turned down "Great Balls of Fire." The stop-start intro of "Great Balls of Fire" was reminiscent of the intro to "Blue Suede Shoes," suggesting Perkins could have had a hit with it, though perhaps not as big as Jerry Lee Lewis's. "According to Perkins, he was given a choice of two songs to perform in Jamboree, both of them published by Helen Range, but I thought both of them was drunk, and he'd chosen the one that was slightly less awful."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.body: This was Carl Perkins' sole hit song at the time. Despite its success, Perkins continued making records every bit as good as this one throughout the rest of 1956. "Karl Perkins, who spent the rest of 1956 making records that were every bit as good as his one hit, Blue Swade Shoes."
